# Worksheet: Getting Started

> ## How to use this worksheet
>
> Work through each part in order, at your own pace. Type every line of code yourself into a **plain R script** — do not copy-paste. Blocks marked **▶ Run this** are code you should type and execute. Blocks marked **✏️ Your turn** ask you to write, modify, or answer something. Boxes marked **🚀 If you finish early** and **Part 14 (Going further)** are optional bonus material.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 1 · Today's question

### Recap

- We are asking whether pine needle length differs between the **sheltered/lee** side and the **exposed/windward** side of a tree.
- The **tree**, not the needle, is our unit of replication — one tree is not enough (this is called **pseudoreplication**).

# Part 2 · Build your project folder

### Why a project folder?

Everything for this project lives in **one folder**, so every file path is *relative* to it — no more hunting for where a file went.

### Create the folder structure

Make a new folder called `pine_project`. Inside it, create three sub-folders:

```         
pine_project/
├── data/       ← your CSV and Excel files go here
├── scripts/    ← your .R code goes here
└── figures/    ← plots you save go here
```

Copy `pine_needles.csv` into `pine_project/data/`.

> ⚠️ **Important:** Leave this copy alone — it is raw data. We will read it but never overwrite it. (Your own field data will get cleaned up and added here starting in Wrangling Your Data.)

✏️ **Your turn:** Full path to your `pine_project` folder: `________________________`

# Part 3 · Orient yourself in Positron

Open your project folder as your workspace: **File → Open Folder…**

Four panes you'll use constantly:

| Pane              | Where       | What it does                   |
|-------------------|-------------|--------------------------------|
| **Editor**        | top-left    | your scripts live here         |
| **Console**       | bottom      | where code actually runs       |
| **Environment**   | right       | every object you've stored     |
| **Plots / Files** | right (tab) | your figures and project files |

# Part 4 · R as a calculator, and storing values

**▶ Run this in the Console:**

``` r
3 + 5
12 / 7
2 ^ 10
sqrt(144)
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** A `+` at the *start* of a console line (instead of the usual `>` prompt) means R is still waiting for you to finish typing something. Press **Esc** to cancel.

Now store a value with the **assignment operator** `<-` (shortcut: Alt/Option + `-`):

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
x <- 7      # store 7 under the name x
x           # read it back
x * 2       # use it in math
```

Look for `x` in the **Environment** pane.


# Part 5 · Naming things well

Good names make code readable months later: be explicit (`needle_length`, not `x2`), never start with a number, and R is **case-sensitive** (`length_mm` ≠ `Length_mm`). Use `lower_snake_case`.

✏️ **Your turn:** Which of these are valid R object names? Circle Y or N.

```         
needle_length     Y / N
3rd_needle        Y / N
Length_mm         Y / N
my.needle.data    Y / N
n_s               Y / N
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 6 · Comments

Anything after `#` is ignored by R — a note for humans.

**▶ Run this in your Script:**

``` r
# average of four needle lengths, in mm
needle_length <- c(20, 21, 23, 25)

mean(needle_length)   # average needle length
```

> 💡 **Key idea:** If a line confused you while writing it, comment *why* you did it — future you will forget.

# Part 7 · Functions and arguments

A **function** is called by name and takes **arguments** in `()`.

**▶ Run this in the Console:**

``` r
sqrt(10)
round(3.14159)             # default: 0 decimal places
round(3.14159, 2)          # 2 decimal places
round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)
```

Stuck? `?round` opens the help page.

# Part 8 · Vectors and data types

A **vector** is a series of values built with `c()`. A spreadsheet column is really just a vector.

**▶ Run this in your Script:**

``` r
length_mm <- c(20, 21, 23, 25)     # numeric vector
side      <- c("n", "s")           # character vector — needs quotes

length(length_mm)   # how many values?
class(length_mm)    # what type?
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** `"n"` in quotes is text. Without quotes, R looks for an *object* called `n` and errors if none exists.

# Part 10 · Load the pine needle data

### Create your script

**File → New File → R Script**. Save it immediately as `01_getting_started.R` inside `pine_project/scripts/`.

**▶ Run this in your Script:**

``` r
# ── Load data ─────────────────────────────
pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_needles.csv")

pine_df    # print to console
```

The path `"data/..."` is *relative* to your project folder — it works on anyone's computer, not just yours.

### Always look before you trust it

**▶ Run each of these:**

``` r
head(pine_df)       # first 6 rows
dim(pine_df)         # (rows, columns)
names(pine_df)       # column names
glimpse(pine_df)     # one line per column: name, type, first values
```

# Part 11 · Your first plot

Every `ggplot` is built from three pieces, joined with `+`: **data**, **aes()** (which columns map to x/y), and a **geom** (how to draw it).

**▶ Run this — the simplest possible plot:**

``` r
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = wind, y = length_mm)) +
  geom_point()
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** The `+` sits at the **end** of a line, never the start.

### Improve it one layer at a time

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = wind, y = length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, color = "tomato") +
  labs(x = "Side of tree",
       y = "Needle length (mm)",
       title = "Needle length by wind exposure")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Make the same plot using `n_s` instead of `wind` on the x-axis. Copy the code above and change what's needed.

``` r
# Write your modified code here:
```

What pattern do you see — does the sheltered or exposed side tend to have longer needles? `________________________`

::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early:** Try `geom_violin()` instead of `geom_boxplot()`, or add `color = group` inside `aes()` to see each field team's data separately.
:::

# Part 12 · Save your plot

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
needle_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = wind, y = length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, color = "tomato") +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)")

ggsave("figures/needle_length.png",
       plot   = needle_plot,
       width  = 3,
       height = 3,
       units  = "in",
       dpi    = 300)
```

Check your `figures/` folder — the PNG should be there.

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** `ggsave()` wants the **filename first**, then `plot =`. Always use `dpi = 300`.

# Part 14 · Going further — optional in class, or take-home if you'd like more practice

> Work through this if you finish early. There are no wrong answers — the goal is to see what `ggplot` can do.

### Histograms, split by group

**▶ Try this:**

``` r
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = length_mm, fill = wind)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, position = position_dodge2(width = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Needle length (mm)", y = "Count", fill = "Side")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Are the two distributions similar in shape, or different? `________________________`

### Facets — one panel per group

``` r
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~group)
```

### Violin plots

``` r
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = wind, y = length_mm, fill = wind)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 2) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Themes — change the look

Add any of these to a plot above:

``` r
+ theme_bw()
+ theme_minimal()
+ theme_classic()
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Which theme do you like best for this kind of biological comparison? Why? `________________________`

# What your finished project folder looks like

```         
pine_project/
├── data/
│   └── pine_needles.csv               <- never touch this
├── scripts/
│   └── 01_getting_started.R           <- your complete script
└── figures/
    └── needle_length.png              <- Part 12
```

This is the structure we will use for **every** analysis this term.

| Folder     | Contents    | Rule                           |
|------------|-------------|--------------------------------|
| `data/`    | raw files   | read-only, never overwrite     |
| `scripts/` | `.R` code   | one script per module          |
| `figures/` | saved plots | always PNG, always `dpi = 300` |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Getting unstuck

When code breaks — and it will, that is normal:

1.  **Read the error message out loud.** R usually names the line and the problem.
2.  **Check the usual suspects:** did you run `library(tidyverse)`? Spelling? A missing `)` or a `+` at the *start* of a line?
3.  `?function_name` opens the built-in help page.
4.  **Bring the exact error** (copy-paste it) to class or office hours.

> 💡 **Key idea:** Every working scientist googles error messages daily. Getting stuck is not failing — it is the job.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
